# The Actor

An actor is a long-running process configured entirely by environment variables. The same binary handles every role — what differs is the topic it subscribes to and the handler it runs.

## Configuration

```{=html}
<div class="env-table">
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_ID</div><div class="env-val">Unique identity of this actor instance.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_TOPIC</div><div class="env-val">Comma-separated list of topics to subscribe to.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_HANDLER</div><div class="env-val">Path to the handler executable invoked per tuple.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_RESULT_TOPIC</div><div class="env-val">Default publish topic for handler output.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_BUS_SUB</div><div class="env-val">NNG pub endpoint to subscribe from. e.g. tcp://bus:5556</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_BUS_PUB</div><div class="env-val">NNG sub endpoint to publish to. e.g. tcp://bus:5557</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_LMDB_PATH</div><div class="env-val">Path to this actor's private LMDB environment.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_TTL_NS</div><div class="env-val">Default tuple TTL in nanoseconds. 0 = no expiry.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_HEARTBEAT_MS</div><div class="env-val">Heartbeat emission interval in milliseconds. Default 5000.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_RETRY_MAX</div><div class="env-val">Max handler retries on non-zero exit. Default 3.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_CONCURRENCY</div><div class="env-val">Messages in flight at once. Default 1, max 32.</div></div>
</div>
```

## Isolation

Optional, opt-in, Linux only. An actor with none of these set behaves exactly as
it did before they existed.

```{=html}
<div class="env-table">
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_UID / ACTOR_GID</div><div class="env-val">Drop to this uid/gid at startup, irreversibly.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_RLIMIT_AS / _CPU / _NOFILE / _NPROC</div><div class="env-val">Resource limits, applied before the privilege drop.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_CGROUP_PATH</div><div class="env-val">Existing cgroup v2 directory to join. Never created by the runtime.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_LANDLOCK_RO</div><div class="env-val">Colon-separated read-only paths. Must cover /bin/sh, the handler and its libraries.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_LANDLOCK_RW</div><div class="env-val">Colon-separated read/write paths. Must contain ACTOR_LMDB_PATH.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_LANDLOCK_NET_CONNECT</div><div class="env-val">Colon-separated outbound TCP ports. Needs Landlock ABI 4 (kernel 6.7+).</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_SECCOMP</div><div class="env-val">1, or permissive_mount when per-tuple namespaces are in use.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_TUPLE_UNSHARE</div><div class="env-val">Namespaces created per handler: pid, ipc, uts, net, mount.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_ROOTFS</div><div class="env-val">pivot_root target. Requires pid and mount in ACTOR_TUPLE_UNSHARE.</div></div>
  <div class="env-row"><div class="env-key">ACTOR_TUPLE_USERNS</div><div class="env-val">Set to 0 to disable the user-namespace fallback for unprivileged unshare.</div></div>
</div>
```

Isolation has two lifetimes. Everything except the last three is **actor-scoped**
— applied once at startup, before the sockets and before any thread, defining
what this actor may ever do. `ACTOR_TUPLE_UNSHARE` and `ACTOR_ROOTFS` are
**tuple-scoped**: created in the forked child and destroyed when the handler
exits.

That second scope is the interesting one. A tuple is a self-contained unit of
work, and the runtime already treats it that way for memory and process
identity. A namespace per tuple extends it to the process tree: when the handler
exits the kernel kills whatever is left inside, so a handler's stray children
cannot outlive the tuple that created them.

Every variable **fails closed**. One that is set but cannot be applied aborts
startup rather than leaving the actor running less confined than configured.

```{mermaid}
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Config      : read environment
  Config --> Isolate  : uid, rlimits, cgroup, Landlock, seccomp
  Isolate --> Connect : NNG + LMDB
  Connect --> Polling
  Polling --> Forking : tuple received
  Forking --> Unshare : fork
  Unshare --> Exec    : per-tuple namespaces
  Exec --> Polling    : handler exits, namespace destroyed
```

## Multi-topic subscription

`ACTOR_TOPIC` accepts a comma-separated list. One actor instance receives tuples on all listed topics, through the same handler, in the order they arrive:

```sh
ACTOR_TOPIC=user_message,sql_result ./actor
```

This is what makes stateful multi-round patterns possible. An actor subscribes to both `user_message` (the initial query) and `sql_result` (the tool response). Both arrive as separate tuple invocations. The correlation ID and LMDB state tie them into a single logical turn — no special runtime support required, just topic subscription.

::: {.callout}
**The handler does not know which topic triggered it.** It reads `stdin` and writes `stdout`. If the handler needs to branch on topic, it reads `ACTOR_TUPLE_ORIGIN` or inspects a field in the payload — that is a handler concern, not a runtime concern.
:::

## Runtime Loop

```{mermaid}
stateDiagram-v2
  [*]        --> Receiving   : open LMDB, connect NNG
  Receiving  --> Receiving   : heartbeat timer fires
  Receiving  --> TTLCheck    : tuple arrives
  TTLCheck   --> Rejected    : expired — publish tuple_rejected
  TTLCheck   --> Inbox       : valid
  Rejected   --> Receiving   : sender notified
  Inbox      --> Forking     : write to LMDB inbox
  Forking    --> Piping      : fork + exec ACTOR_HANDLER, set env vars
  Piping     --> Waiting     : write payload to stdin
  Waiting    --> Reading     : handler exits
  Reading    --> Outbox      : read stdout result
  Outbox     --> Publishing  : write to LMDB outbox
  Publishing --> Receiving   : publish to bus, clear inbox + outbox
```

The runtime is generic and permanent. The handler is specific and ephemeral. Neither knows the other exists beyond a file path and two file descriptors.

## Rejection

No tuple is ever dropped silently. Any drop condition publishes a `tuple_rejected` tuple back on the bus so the original sender can observe and respond.

```json
{
  "tuple_id":        "<uuidv7-hex>",
  "correlation_id":  "<uuidv7-hex>",
  "origin":          "actor-id-who-sent",
  "topic":           "original_topic",
  "reason":          "ttl_expired | payload_cap_exceeded | result_cap_exceeded | max_retries_exceeded"
}
```

| Reason | Condition |
|---|---|
| `ttl_expired` | Tuple arrived after its TTL window |
| `payload_cap_exceeded` | Incoming payload exceeds `ACTOR_MAX_PAYLOAD` |
| `result_cap_exceeded` | Handler result exceeds `ACTOR_MAX_PAYLOAD` |
| `max_retries_exceeded` | Handler returned non-zero after all retry attempts |

Subscribe to `tuple_rejected` to implement dead-letter handling, surface errors to users, or feed observability pipelines.

## Deployment

**Bare process:**

```sh
./mesh-proxy &

ACTOR_ID=worker-1 \
ACTOR_TOPIC=work \
ACTOR_RESULT_TOPIC=result \
ACTOR_BUS_SUB=tcp://localhost:5556 \
ACTOR_BUS_PUB=tcp://localhost:5557 \
ACTOR_HANDLER=./handlers/worker \
ACTOR_LMDB_PATH=/var/actor/worker \
./actor &
```

**Kubernetes (optional):**

```yaml
env:
  - name: ACTOR_ID
    valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
  - name: ACTOR_TOPIC
    value: work
  - name: ACTOR_BUS_SUB
    value: tcp://proxy:5556
  - name: ACTOR_BUS_PUB
    value: tcp://proxy:5557
  - name: ACTOR_HANDLER
    value: /handlers/worker
  - name: ACTOR_LMDB_PATH
    value: /var/actor/lmdb
```

K8s is optional. The runtime has no awareness of it.
